original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: All seven explicit algorithm branches make name point to a string literal and then call strlcpy(name, buf, buflen), treating the literal as the destination. Under the usual strlcpy semantics, when buflen is nonzero and prefix handling has not returned early, buf points to an empty string and the copy still writes a terminating NUL to name; modifying a string literal is undefined behavior and may crash. buflen describes remaining output-buffer capacity and cannot make name a valid writable destination; the post-copy length check cannot prevent the invalid write that already occurred. Reviewed type: reversed copy source and destination, writing to a string literal with undefined behavior.
original_descriptions.security_change: The only difference changes the call to strlcpy(buf, name, buflen), restoring buf as destination and name as source. The order remains rejecting zero capacity, initializing output, writing a prefix and checking truncation when needed, advancing buf and reducing buflen together, then copying the algorithm name into the remaining output space and checking truncation. The destination pointer and its capacity now correspond, blocking writes to the string literal. Reviewed fix mechanism: correct the copy-argument direction so immutable name text is the source and the actual output pointer is the destination, while retaining remaining-capacity and truncation handling synchronized with that destination.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: the local repair clearly establishes that copy source, destination, and destination capacity must correspond. The analysis uses the usual strlcpy semantics and assumes the caller provides buflen writable bytes at buf; the input does not prove that caller precondition. No residual issue in this local mechanism is visible in after, but this does not claim that other call paths or external APIs are completely safe.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: In the double-quoted value branch, strchr(*value + 1, '"') treats the first encountered double quote as the terminator, including a quote escaped by a backslash. The old code writes NUL there and sets *cp to the following byte. For a value containing an escaped quote, this truncates the value and leaves the remainder for later parsing. The existing !end check confirms only that some quote exists and cannot establish that it is an unescaped terminator; the concrete security effect depends on later use of the parse result. Reviewed type: incorrect handling of escaped quotes, truncating the value and misaligning the later parse cursor.
original_descriptions.security_change: after reads the original content through p and writes the compacted content through end. On a backslash, it first advances p and copies the following character, skipping that character's end-quote test; only the ordinary-character path allows an unescaped quote to terminate the scan. On success it writes NUL through end, and end = ++p sets *cp after the raw closing quote, keeping the output-value boundary distinct from the input-consumption position. Reviewed fix mechanism: while parsing escaped-delimiter content, process the escape pair before testing for an unescaped delimiter; during in-place compaction, maintain separate read and write positions and update the later parse cursor from the advanced read position.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: both sides clearly repair the mechanism that misclassified an escaped quote as the value terminator, and the escape semantics are directly supported by the new branch and comment without assuming caller behavior. This does not establish complete safety of after: if a trailing backslash is immediately followed by the string NUL, the loop increments p once, copies NUL, then increments p again and the next while test reads beyond the terminator; crossing the object boundary depends on buffer range. Also, when compaction occurs and no closing quote is found, the loop exits without ensuring that *end is a terminator, and the final check may read a stale character at the original position.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: The old code opens cfg->authpending_file with O_RDONLY | O_CREAT. If the final path component can be replaced by a symbolic link, open follows the link and may create the target when it does not exist; the exact effect depends on path control and permissions. Existing nonempty-path checks, default-path formatting bounds, and open-failure logging do not restrict link resolution. The descriptor is closed only after authentication ends, so if exec occurs meanwhile the old code has no close-on-exec flag; if the target is a terminal and process conditions allow it, it also does not prevent acquisition of a controlling terminal. The source does not prove that these conditions are reachable. Reviewed type: symbolic-link following (CWE-61), descriptor inheritance across exec, and controlling-terminal acquisition risk.
original_descriptions.security_change: The same open now includes O_NOFOLLOW, O_CLOEXEC, and O_NOCTTY, respectively refusing to follow the final symbolic link, closing the descriptor on successful exec, and preventing this open from making a terminal the controlling terminal. These restrictions take effect when the descriptor is acquired, before the later authentication call; open failure still only logs and continues authentication. In addition, after the final debug output at done, the code calls fclose(cfg->debug_file) when cfg->is_custom_debug_file is true, adding cleanup for the custom debug stream. Reviewed fix mechanism: apply path-resolution, exec-lifetime, and terminal-side-effect restrictions directly in open instead of relying only on post-open error handling or close after authentication; perform resource cleanup after its final use under an ownership-related condition.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain and pass: the local security change to the same notification-file open is clear and does not require proving that an attack is reachable. The link risk depends on path influence, while exec and controlling-terminal risks require their respective runtime conditions. O_NOFOLLOW does not block symbolic links in intermediate directories and does not validate object type, owner, or path trust, so after cannot be declared completely safe. Whether debug-stream cleanup satisfies ownership requirements depends on unavailable configuration-initialization semantics; it is not treated as an independently confirmed vulnerability fix.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: After _krb5_extract_ticket returns success, the old code directly copies rep.enc_part, frees reply_key, and returns. Even when ctx->pk_init_ctx exists, this path does not explicitly use a PA-PKINIT-KX confirmation to establish the relationship among the PKINIT context, reply key, and ctx->cred.session. Successful decoding, FAST unpacking, and ticket extraction do not equal this confirmation; if those steps accept a response later rejected by key exchange confirmation, the old path can still return success. The specific cryptographic checks cannot be determined from this function. Reviewed type: missing PKINIT key-exchange confirmation, an incomplete authentication validation.
original_descriptions.security_change: The added logic runs only after ticket extraction succeeds and ctx->pk_init_ctx exists: it searches the AS-REP padata for KRB5_PADATA_PKINIT_KX and passes the search result, PKINIT context, still-unfreed reply_key, and session key to _krb5_pk_kx_confirm. Its return value replaces ret; on confirmation failure, enc_part is no longer copied and the existing cleanup returns an error. Only when confirmation succeeds and the confirmation data is nonempty does the code set KRB5_INIT_CREDS_PKINIT_KX_VALID. Reviewed fix mechanism: before committing an authentication result, correlate the existing protocol context, reply key, extracted session key, and response confirmation data; propagate confirmation failure to the final return and use the same result to block copying later state, releasing the required key only after confirmation completes.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: the local repair clearly incorporates key-exchange confirmation into the success path before releasing the key needed for confirmation. The conclusion is limited to this call and error-propagation relationship, assuming the confirmation helper expresses success or failure through its return; its algorithm and policy for empty confirmation data are not inferred. after does not explicitly check padata before accessing rep.kdc_rep.padata->val and ->len; if earlier processing does not guarantee it is non-null, a conditional null dereference remains. Ticket extraction may also update ctx->cred before a later failure without visible rollback, and the new valid flag is not cleared in this function, so the full state lifetime is not proved safe.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: The old code takes session directly from handle->plugin_handle, reads session->destroyed, and writes session->hangingup. If another thread removes and frees the session in this interval, either member access can use a stale object. A non-null check excludes only NULL; atomic reading of destroyed still requires the object to remain alive and cannot protect the later hangingup write. Global-stop and initialization checks likewise do not guarantee session lifetime. Reviewed type: insufficient session-lifetime synchronization, with possible use after free during concurrent destruction.
original_descriptions.security_change: after first acquires sessions_mutex and then uses janus_videocall_lookup_session(handle) to find the session, placing lookup, the non-null check, destroyed check, and clearing hangingup in one critical section; both early-return paths and the normal path release the lock. If session removal and freeing follow the same mutex protocol, this order prevents a session from being freed concurrently between lookup and completion of member access. Reviewed fix mechanism: resolve the shared object, check its state, and access its members while holding the owning lock, unlocking only after the last access on every exit; an atomic operation on one field cannot replace protection of the object lifetime.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: the local change clearly changes direct session-pointer access to lookup and use under the session lock, establishing the synchronization repair. Lifetime protection depends on removal and freeing using sessions_mutex and the lookup returning a valid session; those implementations are not provided, so actual use-after-free reachability and complete safety of after cannot be proved.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: When attribute_len is 0 but update_len is nonzero, the old code skips bgp_attr_parse but still populates nlris[NLRI_UPDATE]. If the corresponding AFI/SAFI is enabled, it later calls bgp_nlri_parse in update mode and passes only the initialized &attr, because attr_parse_ret remains BGP_ATTR_PARSE_PROCEED. Existing packet-length checks constrain field ranges but do not ensure that ordinary NLRI and attribute data are both present; later NLRI-pointer, length, and AFI/SAFI checks do not establish this relationship. The source confirms this parse path but does not establish a downstream null dereference or crash. Reviewed type: insufficient input-semantics validation, allowing attribute-free ordinary NLRI into update parsing.
original_descriptions.security_change: The registration condition for ordinary NLRI changes from update_len being nonzero to requiring both update_len and attribute_len to be nonzero. When attribute length is zero, the code no longer sets the ordinary-NLRI pointer or length and does not advance the stream position in that branch; the later parse loop skips the entry whose pointer was not set, blocking attribute-free ordinary NLRI from entering update parsing. original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: When name has a vg- prefix, a nonempty machine-name segment, and a trailing group ID accepted by parse_gid, before passes an e - p length with no upper bound directly to strndupa. Under the usual semantics of copying the string on the stack, a very long machine-name segment may exhaust stack space. The earlier checks establish only that delimiters exist and the segment is nonempty; machine_name_is_valid runs after the copy and cannot protect that allocation. The later buflen check protects the output buffer and cannot limit the earlier stack consumption. Reviewed type: input-length-driven stack exhaustion under the usual strndupa semantics.

Reviewed fix mechanism: before any allocation and copy driven by a length derived from input delimiter positions, impose an upper bound; route an excessive segment through the existing failure path so a later content check cannot be asked to undo resource consumption.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: The old code converts the address of local ctrl_sock_id to void * and passes it to FTPs_OS_ServerTaskInit before returning. If that interface or the created task retains the address and dereferences it after FTPs_Init returns, the object lifetime has ended. The NET_SOCK_ID_NONE check excludes only socket-initialization failure, and the rtn_val check handles only task-initialization status; neither extends the parameter object lifetime. Whether the interface synchronously copies the argument is not visible, so an actual dangling access cannot be asserted. Reviewed type: conditional use after return, passing the address of an automatic-storage object to a task-initialization interface.
original_descriptions.security_change: ctrl_sock_id changes from automatic to static storage duration. The order remains obtaining the socket ID, rejecting a failure value, passing its address, and returning; after the change the object remains alive when the function returns, blocking the failure mechanism in which this call ends the parameter address's lifetime. Reviewed fix mechanism: when an outgoing object address may be consumed later, make the object lifetime cover the consumer's access period; after extending lifetime, repeated-call value isolation still requires separate consideration.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: the declaration, address passing, and function return form a clear local lifetime repair without requiring proof of actual attack reachability. The old error requires the recipient to access the address after function return, which the input does not establish. after shares the static object across all calls and later calls overwrite it; if initialization can repeat or run concurrently, an existing task may read an overwritten value, and the input shows no corresponding isolation or synchronization. This does not establish complete safety of after.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: gfcm initially receives gfs->global and is replaced by the local color table only when gfi and its local table are non-null. If the global table is null and no local table is selected, the color->haspixel == 2 branch directly reads gfcm->ncol to compare the pixel, dereferencing a null pointer. The existing gfi/local checks protect only local-table selection; the pixel-range comparison itself must dereference gfcm and cannot protect a missing table. Another branch passes null gfcm to Gif_FindColor, whose null-pointer behavior is not defined by the input. Reviewed type: null-pointer dereference (CWE-476).
original_descriptions.security_change: The pixel-value branch first checks !gfcm and uses logical-or short-circuiting to skip gfcm->ncol when the table is absent, returning color->pixel directly; when the table exists, the original range comparison remains. The color-lookup branch calls Gif_FindColor only when gfcm is non-null; otherwise it sets index to -1 and follows the existing conditional warning and return path. Reviewed fix mechanism: select an optional resource first and then handle its absence according to the operation: use a null check to short-circuit member access when an existing pixel value is available, and skip lookup with a failure result when a color table is required. Preserve the original comparison and lookup flow when the resource exists.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: before computes the pixel-region length as pixmap_height * bytes_per_line, adds it to the header and color-table lengths, and compares the total with file_data_len. If the multiplication overflows in the operand types, the comparison uses a corrupted length; the outer addition involving sizeof cannot recover high bits lost by the completed multiplication. The existing row-stride lower bound constrains one row only, and its width multiplication also has no explicit widening. The function then stores image_data and returns success, potentially passing an undersized mapping to later processing; actual pixel reads are not shown, so an out-of-bounds access cannot be asserted here. Reviewed type: integer overflow in length calculation that may cause the mapped image-data size check to underestimate the image size.
original_descriptions.security_change: after first bounds the header size and color-table entry count, then bounds pixel depth, width, height, and row stride, making inputs to the per-row length calculation finite. Before the final mapping-length check, it casts bytes_per_line to gsize so the full pixel-region multiplication is not first evaluated in a narrower field type. The color-table length check and image_data offset both change from n_colors to color_map_entries, keeping these uses on the same field. Unpacking changes to per-field macro calls, with window coordinates using an S32 macro; the macro definitions are not given, so this is not treated as another established memory-safety repair. Reviewed fix mechanism: bound external fields before using them in size calculations, widen an operand before multiplication, validate the complete mapping length, and only then publish the data pointer. The total-limit check itself must use safe arithmetic; using one count field consistently for the check and offset provides internal consistency but cannot validate the field's file-format semantics.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain as a local arithmetic repair pair. The necessary assumptions are that ASSERT_HEADER stops execution when its condition fails and that the target platform's gsize can represent the bounded total; this does not prove safety on every platform. after still computes bytes_per_line * pixmap_height directly in the total limit check, and the 1UL on the other side does not widen that left multiplication, so narrow field arithmetic may still overflow. If gsize is also too small, the final check remains at risk. The input does not provide color-table layout rules, so changing to color_map_entries cannot be confirmed as matching the actual file layout; that field replacement is not separately treated as a verified repair.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: The function calls streamIteratorStart on local iterator si, then streamIteratorGetID, and returns without calling the corresponding Stop. If the iterator holds resources requiring explicit release, they may remain allocated after every call. The existing !found branch only assigns a sentinel to edge_id and does not end iteration; both the path where an ID is found and the path where no ID is found omit cleanup. Reviewed type: missing iterator-lifetime cleanup, with potential resource leak.
original_descriptions.security_change: After the ID query and the edge_id assignment for a not-found result, the code unconditionally calls streamIteratorStop(&si). The call is outside the !found branch, so both paths end the same iterator before returning and complete the Start, GetID, Stop sequence. Reviewed fix mechanism: after starting a local query object and completing the lookup, perform its corresponding end operation at the branch join so every result path completes lifetime cleanup.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain as a local lifetime repair pair. The two sides establish that Stop was omitted after iterator start and that the change covers both return paths. A resource leak requires this iterator to need explicit termination; Start and Stop implementations are not provided, so resource type, release details, and leak size are not inferred. No other directly confirmable unresolved issue is visible, and this does not claim complete safety of after.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: After obtaining session_info, the old code checks only non-nullness and HANDSHAKING state and does not bind FINISH processing to session_info->use_psk. A selected PSK session that satisfies the preceding conditions can therefore enter later FINISH-request handling. The connection-level KEY_EX_CAP check does not establish that the current session is non-PSK, and the handshake-state check does not distinguish session modes. When later conditions hold, this path resets the message buffer, appends FINISH data, and performs signature/HMAC validation; the function does not establish that validation succeeds or that authentication is bypassed. Reviewed type: incomplete protocol-state validation, failing to exclude PSK sessions from FINISH processing.
original_descriptions.security_change: After successful session lookup and the null check, the code adds a use_psk check; when true it returns SPDM_ERROR_CODE_UNEXPECTED_REQUEST. This return occurs before reading handshake state and before subsequent FINISH-message processing, so a PSK session cannot enter those operations through this function; non-PSK sessions continue through the original checks. Reviewed fix mechanism: when handling a session-specific protocol message, first confirm that the session exists and then verify that its negotiated mode permits the message; reject a mode-mismatched session before message-buffer or cryptographic processing. Connection capability, session existence, and handshake stage cannot replace a session-mode check.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: the local repair is clear—an explicit mode condition on the same session blocks the PSK path that before allowed FINISH processing. The trigger requires a session to pass the preceding conditions; no external reachability or cryptographic success need be proven. after still reads the request header before checking request_size, and response capacity remains protected only by an assertion; these properties depend on unavailable caller constraints and macro semantics and are outside this change, so after is not declared completely safe.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: When added != 0, the function calls mark_adjust() to adjust marks and difference entries. If that call invalidates the saved dp, the old code may still write through dp->df_count[idx_to] or continue traversal through dp->df_next. dfree == NULL means only that this branch did not proactively unlink the entry; it does not prove dp remains valid after mark_adjust(), and the loop-entry dp != NULL check does not prove that the node is still alive. The freeing mechanism and trigger are not shown in the input. Reviewed type: invalid-pointer use, potentially a use after free if the node has been released (CWE-416).
original_descriptions.security_change: After mark adjustment, change notification, and dfree cleanup, the code adds an added != 0 && !valid_diff(dp) check; failure exits the difference traversal immediately, preventing later count write-back and list access. The old else becomes an independent if (dfree == NULL), so the validity check covers both the path where dp remains the original node and the path where active removal leaves it pointing to a successor. Reviewed fix mechanism: when a call may change the validity of a container node referenced across it, do not substitute a local deletion flag or non-null test for a liveness check; validate the node after the call and before dereferencing it again, and terminate when the continuation point is uncertain.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: both sides clearly show a node-validity check before continuing the same difference traversal after a potentially invalidating modification. The necessary assumption is that valid_diff(dp) can safely determine whether this node remains valid; its implementation and mark_adjust invalidation path are not provided, so actual attack reachability or inevitable use after free is not asserted. The added check occurs after changed_lines() and optional diff_fold_update(), so it does not establish that those calls or other paths are completely safe.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: In a DTLS-enabled build, a packet whose first byte is 20 through 63 and whose dtls->ssl is non-null directly stops the timeout timer, may switch to passive-handshake state, and passes len bytes from buf to BIO_write and SSL_read. Even with ICE enabled, the old code does not first check whether ICE media has started or whether source sa matches an active remote candidate. The non-null SSL check confirms only that a session exists; the later PJPROJECT receive branch cannot protect a DTLS packet already processed and returned. Traffic that violates ICE state or source conditions can therefore affect the handshake or consume processing resources; the exact denial-of-service effect depends on external state and library behavior. Reviewed type: missing ICE-state and packet-source constraints before DTLS processing, potentially causing denial of service.
original_descriptions.security_change: In the same DTLS branch, before timer and SSL-state operations, the code adds gating: when rtp->ice is non-null, ice_media_started must be true or the function returns 0; it then iterates ice_active_remote_candidates, comparing at most PJ_ICE_MAX_CAND candidates and allowing the packet only when ast_sockaddr_cmp_addr(&candidate->address, sa) returns 0. With no match it returns 0. A rejected packet therefore cannot continue to stop the timer, switch handshake role, or enter BIO_write/SSL_read; the original path remains when ICE is not enabled. Reviewed fix mechanism: before protocol data enters a stateful handler, associate the existing session check with negotiated state and receive source—check state, compare the actual source with active candidates, return immediately on failure, and permit timer, handshake, and SSL-input operations only on success.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: the local relationship between the new state/source gates and the original DTLS operations is clear, without needing to prove actual attack reachability. The exact address fields compared are determined by the external API, so this does not claim port validation or authentication. after relies on active-candidate storage being valid whenever ice_media_started is true, which is supported only by a comment. The loop obtains a candidate before checking the count limit; if the bound is reached while the iterator returns a held reference, the object is not released in the loop, creating a conditional reference-leak concern. Both versions also read *in when len has not been ruled out as zero. The new ICE code has no separate HAVE_PJPROJECT guard, so build compatibility requires external definitions. These limits do not negate this local repair.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: After a REQUEST_QUEUED or REQUEST_RUNNING timeout, the old code sets a stop state and waits for the child only when have_children is true and child_pid is not NO_SUCH_CHILD_PID; otherwise it directly changes child_state to REQUEST_DONE and enters cleanup, where a particular CoA request is freed immediately. Comparing the thread identifier does not prove that the request has left the queue or is no longer referenced by a worker; if such references remain, cleanup may cause use after free. The reference condition and actual concurrent interleaving cannot be established from this function alone. In addition, a queued DETAIL request continues waiting even after its deadline. Reviewed type: request-lifetime state error, with potential premature cleanup and use after free.
original_descriptions.security_change: The new code first handles the inconsistent case of a thread disabled while the request is still queued or running. In the enabled-thread path, it waits only when now is less than received plus max_request_time, removes the timeout exemption for queued DETAIL requests, and applies the delay limit to every request on this path. On timeout it first sets REQUEST_STOP_PROCESSING, then selects wait_for_child_to_die, and finally schedules a callback through common INSERT_EVENT; child_pid now decides only whether to log and no longer whether direct cleanup is permitted. The forced deletion path changes to REQUEST_DONE and runs through cleanup, so a stop request and wait for processing to finish precede later reclamation. Reviewed fix mechanism: do not substitute absence of a worker identifier for confirmation that a request lifetime has ended. For an object still marked queued or running, publish a stop state on timeout, enter a wait-for-completion callback, and avoid directly rewriting completion state and cleaning up; a wait deadline must not be unconditionally bypassed for one request category.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: within the same request-state branch, the local lifetime repair is clear—from inferring cleanup from a thread identifier to uniformly requesting stop and entering a wait callback after timeout. A use-after-free consequence is conditional on the queue or worker still referencing request; actual attack reachability is not asserted. wait_for_child_to_die is not provided, so final reclamation safety is not established. In the no-thread exceptional path, if rad_assert returns or is disabled, callback can remain null and execution can reach final release; the new assertion alone does not prove that path safe. Delay growth followed by clamping also has no visible arithmetic-overflow protection, but types and ranges are unknown, so overflow is not asserted.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: In the P1-P6 branches, the code passes the s returned from parsing width directly to parse height; P2, P3, P5, and P6 also pass the s returned from parsing height to parse maxval. If an earlier call returns NULL, the next skip_int receives a null pointer. Whether that causes a null dereference depends on the unavailable skip_int implementation. The old have_wh flag is set to 1 immediately after attempting a parse and does not mean both fields were read successfully; numeric checks after the loop cannot prevent the earlier null-pointer propagation. Reviewed type: unchecked parse return value passed to a later parse operation.
original_descriptions.security_change: have_wh is removed, and width and height being zero determine which field remains to be parsed. After parsing width, the code verifies that s is non-null, points to a nonzero character, and width is positive before parsing height. If parsing height returns NULL, it continues to the next line only when the current line successfully parsed the preceding field; otherwise it returns. Other failure cases also return before parsing maxval. maxval is likewise checked for NULL first, then *s, and only then enters the original numeric-range validation. allow_null resets on each line, tying cross-line retry to progress made on that line. Reviewed fix mechanism: in chained parsing, validate the returned cursor and the field already parsed before passing the cursor to the next parser; limit cross-line retry to a line with parsing progress, and on failure either continue outer input or return so a failed cursor cannot flow into the next operation.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: the unchecked-return propagation and its block in the same P1-P6 parse chain are directly visible and pass as a local repair. A null dereference is only a conditional inference. Cross-line state behavior assumes width and height start at zero and that skip_int uses the stated output behavior when no field is read; those constraints are not supplied. after still does not initialize fields at entry or clear ph->ok, so reuse of the structure and early-EOF cases are not proved safe.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: The old code allows a URL whose protocol parses as file and passes the URL-form check to reach s->io_open with AVIO_FLAG_READ. Existing protection constrains the protocol and its URL form but not the file extension. If a caller can supply a URL for an unintended local file, this function does not reject it because its extension is disallowed; the readable range and any later disclosure depend on the call environment. Reviewed type: insufficient local-file read restriction, with a missing file-extension policy.
original_descriptions.security_change: After protocol parsing succeeds, the repair handles the file-prefixed proto_name branch first: when c->allowed_extensions is not "ALL" and av_match_ext(url, c->allowed_extensions) is false, it logs an error and returns AVERROR_INVALIDDATA. Only an allowed extension continues to the original URL-form validation and read-only open, blocking a mismatched-extension file URL before opening. The HTTP branch does not use this policy. Reviewed fix mechanism: refine protocol permission into a file-resource policy by identifying the file branch, honoring an explicit allow-all configuration only when present, matching the original URL against the permitted extension set, and returning on mismatch before the existing URL check and open.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: the policy tightening on the same file-open path is clear and can be extracted as applying a resource-class restriction after protocol permission but before opening the resource. The impact assumes URL input can be influenced by an unexpected source; extension-config defaults and the full matcher semantics are not provided. after explicitly allows "ALL", and an allowed extension does not prove the file is safe. In addition, both versions have early returns after av_dict_copy that bypass av_dict_free(&tmp); if tmp was allocated, it may still leak, including on the new rejection path.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: In the old version, when a callback or parse-state operation returns failure, it calls AcpiPsCompleteThisOp only for the current Op once and returns; on the normal completion path and in the termination cleanup loop, failure of that call also returns immediately. If scopes still need to be popped, execution bypasses later AcpiPsPopScope and completion of outer Ops. The non-null Op check protects only the current entry, and failure checks trigger early exit without ensuring the scope stack is cleaned. Whether this leaves actual memory or other resources depends on unavailable cleanup APIs and ownership. Reviewed type: incomplete error-path cleanup, potentially leaving resources behind.
original_descriptions.security_change: The new version uses Ascending to control whether the ascending callback continues and stores the return result separately in ReturnStatus. On termination, callback failure, or failure completing the current Op, it closes the ascending callback but continues completing the current operation and popping scopes, then processes later Ops until Op is null. Failure of the completion operation no longer immediately truncates this cleanup loop; an existing error takes priority, while a completion error can replace a success or termination status. A termination status is also retained as AE_CTRL_TERMINATE instead of being changed to AE_OK. Reviewed fix mechanism: separate business-callback execution state from the final return state; record the error and disable later business callbacks, let the common cleanup loop continue, and return according to error priority so cleanup failure or business failure does not truncate cleanup of remaining objects.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: the two versions clearly establish a local repair from early error return to continuing scope unwinding, without assuming a particular release implementation. Resource leakage is stated only conditionally. In the new AE_CTRL_PENDING branch, AcpiPsCompleteOp failure still returns directly, so that exit path is not covered; this also does not prove that cleanup APIs have released resources after failure.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: After pam_authenticate on local_auth succeeds, the old code calls pam_end and returns status = 0 when that succeeds. If credential authentication succeeds but account-management checks should reject the account, the old path never obtains or evaluates that result. Checking pam_authenticate only constrains the authentication step and does not establish that account management also passed. Reviewed type: missing account-authorization check, entering the success path based only on identity authentication.
original_descriptions.security_change: After successful pam_authenticate and before pam_end, the code calls pam_acct_mgmt on the same local_auth with PAM_SILENT | PAM_DISALLOW_NULL_AUTHTOK. Every non-PAM_SUCCESS result returns early: PAM_AUTH_ERR, PAM_USER_UNKNOWN, and PAM_NEW_AUTHTOK_REQD map to status = 1, while other failures map to status = 2. An account-management failure therefore cannot continue along this path to status = 0. Reviewed fix mechanism: make credential authentication and account permission two sequential gates; after authentication succeeds, check the same session's account status, convert every failure to a non-success return, and only then allow session termination and final success.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: the complete function directly shows the account-management result becoming a necessary condition of the success path, establishing the local repair. The actual rejection depends on account policy; the input does not prove a particular account state or attack reachability. Like the original authentication-failure branch, each new failure branch returns after pam_start succeeds without calling pam_end, so cleanup may still be incomplete; this repair does not resolve it and the resource effect cannot be determined from these texts alone.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: When log_fp is empty, the old code opens log_file with fopen(log_file, "a+") and checks only whether opening failed. If the path is replaced by a symbolic link, points through a hard link to another file, or names an openable non-regular object, the function can still return a stream for that object and later logging may affect an unintended target. The actual effect depends on path control and later writes, since this function does not write the log directly. FD_CLOEXEC limits descriptor inheritance across exec but cannot validate the file target. Reviewed type: insufficient link-following and file-object validation while opening a log file (CWE-59).
original_descriptions.security_change: The new branch first opens log_file with O_NOFOLLOW, refusing to follow a symbolic link in the final path component, and requests owner read/write permissions for a newly created file. It wraps the same descriptor with fdopen and then checks the opened object with fstat(fh, &st). If the query fails, the link count is not 1, or the object is not regular, it clears log_fp, closes the descriptor, and returns NULL; only after these checks does it set FD_CLOEXEC and return the stream. This ties path opening and object validation to one descriptor and keeps a disallowed object from reaching the normal return path for later logging. Reviewed fix mechanism: restrict final-component link following during path open, validate object type and link count through the same open descriptor, block normal stream return on failure, and deliver the stream only after validation.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: the new opening branch in the same function has a clear local repair relationship without requiring actual attack reachability. Link-count checking reflects only the check-time state, O_NOFOLLOW does not exclude symlinks in intermediate directories, and existing permissions and ownership are not validated. The cached log_fp is still returned directly. after also has visible resource-cleanup issues: fdopen failure does not close fh, and validation failure after fdopen only calls close(fh) without releasing the FILE stream. Validation occurs after opening and cannot undo effects of opening a special file.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: In the branch compiled without HAVE_LOGIN_CAP_H, the old code conditionally calls setuid only; it neither sets the target primary or supplementary groups nor checks setuid's return value. Thus, even if the UID switch succeeds, command execution may retain group privileges not belonging to the target user; if the switch fails, execution still proceeds to execvpe under the unswitched identity. Earlier permit and authentication controls do not prove that the process credentials actually changed, while setusercontext error handling exists only in the other build branch. Reviewed type: incomplete privilege switching and ignored failure (CWE-273, CWE-250).
original_descriptions.security_change: After successfully querying the target passwd entry, the no-HAVE_LOGIN_CAP_H branch now sets the target GID, initializes supplementary groups using the target username and primary group, and then switches the target UID. On platforms with the relevant support, setresgid/setresuid set real, effective, and saved IDs; other platforms use setregid/setreuid. Every -1 return reports an error and exits, so group setup completes before dropping user privileges and a failed credential switch cannot continue to command execution. The original unchecked conditional setuid block is removed. Reviewed fix mechanism: realize the authorized target identity as actual execution credentials—query the account, set primary and supplementary groups, then switch user IDs, terminating immediately on any failure and allowing command execution only after all steps succeed.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: both sides directly show a local repair in the same credential-switch branch and pass. The consequences require the no-HAVE_LOGIN_CAP_H branch to be compiled, original group permissions to differ from the target, or identity switching to fail; actual attack reachability need not be proven. The fallback uses setregid/setreuid, whose saved-ID behavior still depends on platform semantics, so all platforms cannot be claimed equivalent; this also does not establish safety of other function paths.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: The input lzw_cs is not range-checked before being used as a signed integer shift count and then used again in codesize = lzw_cs + 1 for another shift. A bit count outside the type range or a result that violates signed-shift rules causes undefined behavior. Even when the shifts are valid, if clear exceeds the actual number of elements in g->codes, the initialization loop writes beyond prefix, first, and suffix. The old avail < 4096 check constrains only later dictionary appends and cannot protect the preceding shifts or initialization; first and code <= avail checks likewise occur after those operations. Reviewed type: input-driven shift undefined behavior and conditional dictionary-array out-of-bounds write.
original_descriptions.security_change: After reading lzw_cs and before any related shift or dictionary initialization, after rejects lzw_cs > gif_lzw_max_code_size, sets an error state, and jumps to return, blocking dangerous operations for that input range in execution order. The dictionary-append limit also changes from 4096 to 1 << gif_lzw_max_code_size, so input and append limits reference the same parameter; its value is not given, so equality of old and new numeric bounds cannot be asserted. Reviewed fix mechanism: validate an external exponent parameter before calculating a shift or using its result as a loop bound, and make the later dictionary-append bound use the same configuration parameter. Parameter range, shift validity, and actual array capacity must still agree.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: Both branches insert name directly into a single-quoted string in the WHERE clause, and the unencrypted branch also inserts value directly into the SET clause. If input contains content that closes the string and changes SQL syntax, sqlite3_exec executes it as SQL and may change the update range or execute additional statements. Checking asprintf's return value handles formatting failure only and does not separate data from SQL syntax; the encrypted branch also leaves name unprotected. Reviewed type: SQL injection (CWE-89).
original_descriptions.security_change: Both branches now use fixed SQL with two placeholders: they prepare the statement, bind value and name separately, and then call step. Parameter content no longer participates in SQL parsing, blocking the original string-concatenation injection path. The encrypted value is now freed after finalize rather than after formatting, keeping it alive during binding and execution. Reviewed fix mechanism: determine SQL structure with a fixed template, bind data by placeholder index, execute, and keep referenced binding data alive until statement completion before freeing it.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: both sides clearly change the same UPDATE from string interpolation to parameter binding, establishing the local repair. These issues do not negate the shown injection repair and do not establish complete safety of after.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: size is accumulated from consecutive length bytes in the input. The old code checks only that the bitstream has at least size bytes remaining and, when buffer is non-null, passes buffer and size to gf_bs_read_data. If the input has enough data but size exceeds the destination capacity, this may write out of bounds. The earlier mux_size check compares declared multiplexed-data length with input remaining data and cannot prove that buffer can hold size. Reviewed type: missing destination-side upper bound on payload length, potentially causing an out-of-bounds write.
original_descriptions.security_change: The existing input-remaining check now also rejects size > LATM_DMX_MAX_SIZE. On excess it first rolls back to pos - 3 and returns GF_FALSE, so nb_bytes is not updated and the later read of size bytes into buffer is not executed; size equal to the limit remains allowed. The fix relates input-derived length to the maximum permitted destination length. Reviewed fix mechanism: before using an input-derived length for a destination write, constrain both available input and the permitted destination-size upper bound; return before publishing the length or writing data on failure.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: the local length restriction clearly corresponds to later operations using the same size and buffer. To interpret this as preventing a destination out-of-bounds write, buffer must have at least LATM_DMX_MAX_SIZE capacity; the input does not provide the macro value, allocation, or caller constraints, so arbitrary buffers are not claimed safe. after also does not explicitly protect accumulation overflow in size or verify that the payload read stays within pos + mux_size; their consequences cannot be determined from this function alone.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: When *state == CCS_VALUE and *type == CCV_SB, the old code directly converts the pending value *vs to int and passes it to BITSET_SET_BIT on cc->bs. If *vs > 0xff, it exceeds the upper bound used by the function's single-byte range branch. The existing check is only in the same-type CCV_SB branch of CCS_RANGE and cannot protect this single-value operation. Whether an actual out-of-bounds write occurs depends on unavailable macro implementation, bitset capacity, and conversion result; the source directly proves only that an over-limit value reaches the bitset operation without rejection. Reviewed type: missing upper-bound check on a single-byte bitset index, potentially causing an out-of-bounds write.
original_descriptions.security_change: In the same CCS_VALUE/CCV_SB branch, before conversion and the bitset operation, the code checks *vs > 0xff and returns ONIGERR_INVALID_CODE_POINT_VALUE when true. That path therefore does not execute BITSET_SET_BIT or the final pending-value and type update; values within the bound retain the original flow. Reviewed fix mechanism: identify the actual write path by state and data type, validate the pending value's representable-domain upper bound before converting it to a bitset index, and return early on an anomaly instead of relying on a check in another state branch.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: the local relationship is clear and can be extracted as an upper-bound check on the pending single-byte value before bitset use. No caller guarantee that *vs is valid is assumed, and actual attack reachability is not asserted. Macro definitions, type widths, and bitset layout are not provided, so the concrete memory consequence remains conditional. after's mixed-type range branch still truncates only the endpoint to 0xff and does not explicitly bound the start *vs; its safety depends on unavailable range-operation semantics and is not proved by this repair.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: The function opens the file with fopen(filename, "w") and writes history strings from history line by line. Under usual POSIX permission semantics, a newly created file inherits permissions filtered by the process's existing umask; if that umask permits other users to read, history content may be exposed. An existing file with permissive permissions is not tightened by this open. The old fp == NULL check tests only whether opening succeeded and cannot guarantee access permissions on the output object. Reviewed type: CWE-732, improper permissions on a history file, potentially exposing history content.
original_descriptions.security_change: The code saves the original umask and sets a mask that blocks group and other permissions before calling fopen, then restores the original umask including on the open-failure path. After a successful open, before writing history it calls chmod to set the filename's permissions to owner read/write only. The first step constrains creation-time permissions; the second tightens permissions on an existing file when the path still refers to the opened file. Reviewed fix mechanism: restrict creation permissions before opening, restore the process's original mask afterward, and tighten target permissions before writing sensitive content, distinguishing creation-time restrictions from changes to an existing file.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: both sides clearly repair permissions on the same history-file write and establish the local relationship. The conclusion uses usual POSIX permission semantics, while exposure depends on original permissions and history content. after does not check chmod's return value and changes permissions by path, so a path change may cause it to modify a file other than the one represented by fp; an existing file can remain permissive until chmod. umask is process-global, and concurrent file creation is not coordinated here. This does not establish complete safety of after.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: When skip_cache is false and a token hits the cache, before directly copies the cached email and returns EVHTP_RES_OK even if the cached repo_id differs from the current request repo_id. The non-null request-header check proves only that a token exists, and the mutex protects cache operations only; neither binds the token to the target repository. This path bypasses the later query that receives both repo_id and token, so the same token used for a different repository can incorrectly reuse another repository's authorization result. Reviewed type: missing resource binding in authorization validation, with a cache hit not checked against the repository.
original_descriptions.security_change: The only textual change adds strcmp(token_info->repo_id, repo_id) == 0 to the successful cache branch. While holding the lock, after first confirms the cache entry exists and then compares cached and requested repositories; only a match copies email and returns success. On mismatch it unlocks and performs the query with the current repo_id and token; if that returns NULL it removes the cache entry and returns FORBIDDEN, otherwise it creates a cache record for the current repository. This blocks a cross-repository cache entry from directly producing success. Reviewed fix mechanism: before reusing a credential-indexed cache result, compare the resource identifier saved in the cache with the current target resource; on mismatch, leave the cache-success path and validate credentials together with the target resource.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: the source directly shows repo_id stored in the cache while the old cache-success path did not use it; the added comparison clearly repairs that resource-binding omission. strcmp requires both repository identifiers to be valid, non-null, NUL-terminated strings, and caller constraints are not shown. Both versions write expire_time, but this function does not check cache expiration; whether an external component maintains it is unknown. This conclusion does not cover underlying-query authorization or overall safety of after.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: In the block-cipher branch, when tls_verify_padding(tls, last) returns a negative value, the old code returns that error immediately and skips MAC extraction, computation, and comparison. When padding passes and the final buffer is large enough for the MAC, it performs those operations. If an external observer can measure processing time, this difference based on post-decryption padding state may reveal whether padding is valid. Existing MAC-length and MAC checks occur after the early return and cannot remove the difference. Reviewed type: timing side channel from early padding-error return, a conditional padding-oracle risk.
original_descriptions.security_change: A padding failure now sets pad_len = 0 instead of returning immediately, so the path continues through later processing. It does not subtract padding length and still extracts a MAC from the tail of last using suite->mac_len; when the length check passes and the MAC length is nonzero, it computes and compares the MAC. This unifies part of the execution flow that previously skipped MAC work on padding failure, but does not establish constant-time behavior. Reviewed fix mechanism: replace immediate exit after a secret-dependent check failure with a continuation length and shared authentication flow, reducing work differences between this and other authentication failures; failure state must remain represented and the common path must still be checked for early exits.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: the local timing repair relationship is clear without requiring proof of actual attack reachability. Side-channel use requires observable timing, while continued MAC computation requires sufficient final-buffer length and nonzero suite->mac_len. after still has an early return for a too-short MAC, and the constant-time behavior of memcmp cannot be determined from the text. Padding-failure state is also cleared and no independent later rejection is forced; if MAC comparison succeeds, the record can enter tls_new_record. after cannot be claimed completely safe.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: The generic property-copy branch reads index n from this and writes the result to index i in deleted. It exits on NJS_ERROR and sets the target property on NJS_OK; for other return values, the old code skips the target slot. If deleted is a fast array and its allocator did not initialize these slots as holes, deleted->start[i] retains an indeterminate state, after which the result length is set and published as the return value. Existing error handling covers only read failure and cannot guarantee the validity of an unwritten slot; the length limit also does not initialize it. The concrete later memory effect cannot be determined from this function alone. Reviewed type: conditional use of an uninitialized value because a result-array hole is not explicitly initialized.
original_descriptions.security_change: In the branch after excluding NJS_ERROR where the read result is not NJS_OK, after first checks deleted->object.fast_array and then calls njs_set_invalid on deleted->start[i]. This occurs before setting the result length and publishing the return value, so a fast-array slot without a copied source value has an explicit state. Successful-copy paths and non-fast result objects remain unchanged. Reviewed fix mechanism: when constructing a result container with holes, handle success, read error, and no-value results for each target position; for no value, explicitly mark the hole according to the target storage representation, then set the length and publish the container instead of initializing only positions with actual values.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain and pass local repair review: both sides clearly correspond to the same property-copy loop, and the change completes state handling for an unwritten target slot. The risk requires an allocator that does not preinitialize slots and a non-success, non-error return meaning the property is absent; the relevant API implementations are not provided, so actual reachability or a concrete memory corruption is not asserted. original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: The loop converts each text segment returned by getgrset with strtol to long, excludes only LONG_MIN and LONG_MAX, and then casts to gid_t. Other negative values and values outside the representable gid_t range may still pass; whether the value changes depends on the actual gid_t definition. The converted value then participates in primary-group deduplication and may be written to groups. ngroups >= maxgroups limits the number of array writes but cannot ensure that each group identifier is numerically valid. Reviewed type: improper integer-range validation, allowing a group identifier to change during conversion to gid_t.
original_descriptions.security_change: The parse variable changes from long to long long and the parser from strtol to strtoll. Before conversion to gid_t, the code rejects ll < 0 or ll > UID_MAX. On a match it sets failure state and jumps to out, frees cp, updates the count, and returns, preventing the value from reaching primary-group comparison or array storage. The capacity check is unchanged. Reviewed fix mechanism: parse text into an intermediate integer, validate that value against the target identifier's allowed interval, and only then convert, deduplicate, and store; capacity and numeric bounds independently constrain write location and write value.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: both sides clearly change endpoint-only parser checks into validation of the target identifier range, establishing a local repair. Rejection of negative values is directly supported; whether the upper bound covers every gid_t conversion risk depends on the unavailable UID_MAX definition and its relationship to gid_t, so complete repair is not claimed. after still does not use an end pointer to validate the entire text or check errno; empty or trailing-character strings may still be accepted. Both versions also have an early maxgroups <= 0 return that bypasses free(cp); if that returned object requires release, this path remains a leak.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: On each call, the old code searches for & starting from var->ptr. If it does not find the delimiter and eof is false, it returns without advancing var->ptr or recording how much was scanned. If the same incomplete field is appended in chunks and repeatedly passed to this function, the already confirmed prefix without & is rescanned; with fixed-size chunks, total scan work can grow quadratically with field length. The entry ptr >= end check excludes only an empty range and does not prevent this repeated work. Reviewed type: algorithmic complexity problem from repeated scanning, with conditional CPU resource exhaustion.
original_descriptions.security_change: The code adds start = var->ptr + var->already_scanned so delimiter search skips the prefix already scanned. When no delimiter is found and input is not finished, it records end - ptr before returning; after processing a field, it advances ptr and resets already_scanned to zero, keeping progress synchronized with the current field start. Key-value parsing still uses the original field start. Reviewed fix mechanism: preserve scan progress relative to the current record start during incremental parsing; save progress before waiting for more data, scan only the new suffix on the next call, and reset progress after consuming the record and advancing its start.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Retain: the local repair relationship is clear. Resource exhaustion requires the caller to append chunks to the same incomplete field and call repeatedly. The fix also requires already_scanned to start valid, remain within the available length of the current field, and refer to an unchanged scanned prefix; initialization and cross-call buffer maintenance are not shown, and this function does not validate the offset. The existing ptr < end check alone cannot guarantee start is valid, but that does not negate the visible repeated-scan repair.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior: When an ICE candidate is responsive, the old code does not compare rtp_session->from_addr with rtp_session->ice.addr before writing dtls->bytes bytes from dtls->data into read_bio and then calling DTLS state processing. If these fields describe the received packet, data from a different address can enter this path. The existing ready condition returns only when there is no data and the session is not ready, while cand_responsive indicates candidate response state; neither proves that the current input came from the negotiated address. Data-length and pointer checks also do not validate source. Reviewed type: missing binding between DTLS input source and negotiated address in the ICE path.
original_descriptions.security_change: The new code retains the candidate-response restriction for non-ICE_LITE ICE sessions and then compares from_addr with ice.addr for every ICE session. If switch_cmp_addr returns false, it logs and returns, so that input cannot reach BIO_write or later state processing. ICE_LITE is exempted only from the candidate-response restriction, not from the new address comparison. Reviewed fix mechanism: before passing network input to protocol parsing and the state machine, compare its source address with the session's negotiated address and return early on mismatch; candidate liveness cannot replace per-input source binding.

This does not prove attack reachability, a bypass of DTLS cryptographic authentication, or the meaning of SWITCH_TRUE for port comparison. Non-ICE paths remain outside this address check; state-index and pending-buffer assertions are unchanged, so overall safety of those operations is not established.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior:
When the initial iv_size is 0 and isProtected is nonzero, the function reads the constant IV length from input, writes it to key_info[20], and then directly reads that many bytes into key_info+21. The old code does not limit the constant IV length to 8 or 16; if it exceeds the remaining target capacity, an out-of-bounds write may occur. The definition of ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE is not provided, so its exact protection behavior cannot be confirmed; even if it checks remaining input bytes, that does not prove sufficient target capacity. Other paths also accept an initial IV length outside 0, 8, or 16 and return GF_OK.
Type description under current review: insufficient validation of the IV length value; conditional out-of-bounds-write risk in the constant-IV branch
original_descriptions.security_change:
In the constant-IV branch, after the original length decrement and before reading data, only lengths 8 or 16 are allowed; any other value triggers a log, sets key_info[20] to 16, and returns GF_NON_COMPLIANT_BITSTREAM, blocking data writing driven by that length. Outside this branch, only an initial IV length of 0, 8, or 16 is allowed; otherwise an error is returned.
Repair mechanism description under current review: bind an input-controlled length to the values allowed for the field: after reading the length, validate the allowed set before using it to drive a target write and return immediately on failure; also validate the other field path that does not trigger this write, so an invalid length cannot be accepted as a successful parse result.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior:
When se->data.server.userdb is NULL, the old code logs and returns 0 without checking signature-segment length or updating *ret_buffer and *ret_buffer_len. If the caller continues parsing remaining input after a success return, the same signature segment is processed repeatedly and may cause nontermination and resource consumption; the caller's loop is not provided, so this is conditional. The original length check occurs after the early return and has no effect on this branch.
Current review type: a success path does not advance parser input state and may cause an infinite loop and denial of service
original_descriptions.security_change:
The no-user-database branch moves after buffer-length, segment-header, and segment-length checks. Only when PART_SIGNATURE_SHA256_SIZE < pss_head_length <= buffer_len does it advance *ret_buffer by pss_head_length bytes, decrease *ret_buffer_len by the same amount, and return 0. The repair validates the consumed range first, then updates input position and remaining length together, eliminating a success path that consumes no input.
Current review repair-mechanism description: a parser's skip branch must also preserve input-consumption invariants: confirm the segment length is valid and within the remaining buffer, advance the pointer by that same length, reduce remaining length, and only then report success.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Keep and pass: both sides clearly change the same branch from successful return without advancing input to validating segment length and consuming the signature segment. The outer loop need not be shown to establish the local repair. Infinite-loop effect depends on the caller continuing with unconsumed input. after explicitly still permits not validating the signature when no user database exists; this repair does not change that policy or establish complete safety of other paths.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior:
When info is found, section count passes processing, capacity computation passes, and allocation succeeds, the old code directly evaluates info->sections[0]. If info->sections is NULL, the ternary expression dereferences the null array pointer before checking the first element; per-section checks inside the loop cannot protect the array itself. A second issue is that after allocating according to max_decomp_size, the code ultimately sets sec_dat->size to unconstrained info->size. The compressed branch's bytes_left and block-offset checks do not constrain this final length, so the function may return an object whose declared length exceeds allocation; whether later use goes out of bounds is not shown.
Current review type: null-pointer dereference; mismatch between buffer capacity and externally declared length, with potential downstream out-of-bounds access
original_descriptions.security_change:
After zero-section handling and before allocation or any sections index access, after rejects a null info->sections, directly blocking the null-pointer path. It retains the original capacity-range check and, before allocation, rejects a record whose info->size exceeds the product of section count and maximum decompressed size, so the logical length passing the check is bounded by computed total capacity; this relation assumes the product calculation and conversion do not overflow or truncate.
Current review repair-mechanism description: validate the container pointer before reading or testing its elements; before allocation and publishing a buffer, bound declared length by the total capacity used for allocation. Capacity calculation also needs independent arithmetic and type-conversion guarantees; element null checks, block-level remaining length, or assigning a length afterward cannot substitute for those relationships.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior:
The old function allocates psz_text with i_size + 1 - 8 and uses i_size - 8 as both memcpy length and terminator index. When i_size < 8, subtraction may produce a negative value or unsigned wrap; after conversion to copy length it may become huge, and the index may also go out of bounds. When i_size exceeds SIZE_MAX and its type can represent that value, conversion of allocation and copy arguments may truncate and break consistency with the index. The existing NULL check tests only whether allocation returned null and does not validate these length/index relationships. The specific consequence depends on integer types, conversions, and allocation result.
Current review type: invalid length arithmetic boundaries may cause out-of-bounds memory access
original_descriptions.security_change:
Before allocation, the code rejects i_size < 8 or i_size > SIZE_MAX, so later processing handles only a size at least the fixed subtraction amount and no greater than SIZE_MAX. Under the expected semantics of MP4_READBOX_EXIT(0), invalid sizes exit before allocation, copying, or terminator writing; a valid size mathematically represents i_size - 8 text bytes plus one terminator byte.
Current review repair-mechanism description: before one size participates in capacity calculation, copy length, and terminator index, validate that it is at least the subtraction amount and no greater than SIZE_MAX; only then allocate, copy, and write, preserving capacity and access-range relationships.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Keep: the two sides show a clear local size-boundary repair without requiring proof of exploitability. This assumes MP4_READBOX_EXIT(0) terminates current reading as its use implies. i_size's type and macro definitions are not provided, so all intermediate expressions cannot be guaranteed safe, especially i_size + 1; after also does not directly prove p_peek has i_size - 8 readable bytes. These limits do not negate the new boundary's blocking of the original invalid-size path.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior:
The handshake branch directly transfers ownership of message->fragment into unparsedHandshakeData_ and continues reading and appending when a complete message is not decoded. If a short fragment still holds a large underlying allocation, accumulating such fragments can retain far more memory than the effective handshake bytes. The underlying-storage condition is stated by the after comment, but the actual trimming implementation is not provided. Existing spliced-handshake-data checks forbid mixing other content types during an incomplete handshake but do not limit memory occupied by handshake fragments.
Current review type: memory amplification by handshake-fragment buffers may exhaust resources (CWE-400)
original_descriptions.security_change:
The same handshake branch now first takes out the existing handshake buffer and coalesces the current fragment. It uses fragment->length() as copy length: when no buffer exists, it creates one with that length plus 1024 bytes; when existing tail space is insufficient, it reserves more, copies into writableTail(), updates effective length, and puts the buffer back in the queue before the original decoding. The queue changes from retaining raw fragment records to retaining copied effective bytes, breaking the relationship in which every short fragment permanently holds its original large allocation.
Current review repair-mechanism description: while accumulating parsed data, do not retain each input slice and its potentially oversized underlying allocation indefinitely; ensure aggregate-buffer tail space, copy only effective bytes, update length, and then pass it to the parser. Fixed extra space reduces repeated growth and is not a total memory cap.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Keep: both sides clearly show a local resource repair from transferring fragment ownership to copying effective data. Memory amplification requires short fragments to retain large underlying allocations; real exploitability is not asserted. after still imposes no total handshake-byte or buffer-record limit, and the existing TODO remains, so resource-exhaustion risk is not claimed entirely removed. Allocation semantics and overflow at length + 1024 are not provided, so no separate confirmed vulnerability is asserted.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior:
The old code first stores allocated data in sud->directory, then checks whether directory and options have remaining data. If either check fails, it jumps to out, frees data, and returns FALSE while sud->directory still points to the freed buffer. If a caller later frees or accesses the buffer through that field, a double free or use-after-free occurs; caller behavior is not visible. Existing length and terminator checks can reject corresponding format errors but do not revoke a pointer already published.
Current review type: a dangling output pointer remains on an error path; conditional double free or use-after-free
original_descriptions.security_change:
All failure branches now enter err, first clear sud->directory to NULL, then free data and return FALSE, removing the field's reference to a freed buffer on error. The success path returns TRUE directly and retains the allocated buffer for the output field, corresponding to the old behavior of clearing local data to skip its free.
Current review repair-mechanism description: when an output structure references a temporary allocation before processing completes, failure cleanup must revoke its ownership pointer as well; clear the output pointer, release the object, and return failure in that order, while retaining the object on success.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Keep: both sides clearly show release and invalidation of the same allocation on the failure path, sufficient to confirm a local repair. Actual double free or use-after-free depends on the caller using failure output. after may still leave a dangling sud->options when option parsing fails and does not uniformly clear other output fields, so all failed outputs are not claimed safe.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior:
Under the usual semantics of strdupa, the old code copies the entire f on the stack, with allocation growing with string length. If required space exceeds available stack, stack exhaustion may result. assert(f) checks only that the pointer is non-null; a null check after copying cannot provide reliable recovery from stack allocation failure. Path simplification and normalization checks occur after copying and do not bound its length.
Current review type: input-length-driven stack allocation may exhaust the stack
original_descriptions.security_change:
The temporary path copy changes from strdupa to strdup, so it no longer consumes stack space proportional to input length and retains a return -ENOMEM path on allocation failure. p gains an _cleanup_free_ marker expressing automatic-release intent; the pointer obtained by skipping leading slashes is passed directly to unit_name_escape without overwriting p, preserving the allocation base for cleanup. Macro definitions are not provided, so exact cleanup cannot be verified from the fragment alone.
Current review repair-mechanism description: move a temporary copy whose size grows with input from stack allocation to heap allocation that can report failure; check allocation result first, process content second, and separate ownership base from the pointer used after skipping a prefix so it can be freed correctly.

original_descriptions.unsafe_behavior:
When is_signed is nonzero and CMAC calculation succeeds, the function uses memcmp to compare data at the tag position computed with at91_aes_roundup(data_length) against computed_cmac, for length AT91_AES_BLOCK_SIZE_BYTE. memcmp is not guaranteed constant-time; if its timing varies with the first differing byte and that variation is observable, tag-matching information may leak. The existing mismatch-and-exit protection prevents decryption after failed verification but cannot remove timing differences during comparison.
Current review type: potential timing side channel in CMAC comparison
original_descriptions.security_change:
The diff has one change: memcmp(...) becomes !consttime_memequal(...), with the same objects, offset, and length. Under constant-time equality semantics of that interface, fixed-length comparison completes first and the code jumps to exit when unequal; only equality continues to decryption. The repair preserves failure-first control flow and targets timing dependence on the matching position.
Current review repair-mechanism description: at authentication-tag validation, replace a general byte comparison without a constant-time guarantee with constant-time equality and invert the condition so failed validation still exits first and decryption follows only success.
original_descriptions.keep_reason: Keep: the local repair relationship is clear. Necessary assumptions are that consttime_memequal implements constant-time comparison and returns nonzero for equality; its definition is not provided, so the guarantee and real observability are not independently verified. Neither side shows data capacity, readable range for the appended tag, or roundup-overflow handling, so these boundaries cannot be called safe and no separate out-of-bounds issue is asserted; this change does not address them.
